newsitem.title: UK: UK budget leaves interest rates to take the strain.
newsitem.headline: UK budget leaves interest rates to take the strain.

text.p: Wednesday's UK budget places the onus squarely on monetary policy to save Britain from another unsustainable economic boom, analysts said.

They predicted Britain's official 6.5 percent interest rates would hit 7.0 percent by year end and said the Bank of England might opt to raise rates as early as next week to choke nascent inflationary pressures.

Moreover, contrary to the Bank of England's assertion that the budget "helps to address the policy dilemma" facing the UK, Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown's maiden budget has actually exacerbated it by giving sterling yet another boost.
"The overall tightening of 5.5 billion stg looked okay but the split was not what the markets were looking for," said Lehman Brothers economist Michael Dicks.
"Whacking the corporate sector rather than households is not that helpful if what you want to do is slow consumer demand," he said.

Sterling soared to five year highs on the budget and this is likely to worsen the split between the sluggish export-driven manufacturing sector and the booming service and consumer sectors, as exports become even less competitive.

Analysts said the measures introduced by Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown failed to live up to his rhetoric and he had not achieved his aim of easing inflationary pressures without damaging industrial and export prospects.
"Brown talked about correcting the imbalance in the economy, but he didn't introduce the measures to achieve it," CIBC chief economist David Coleman said.

"He didn't deliver what he promised. So it's over to you Mr. George," Coleman said, arguing that the central bank's monetary policy committee led by governor Eddie George would now have to raise interest rates.
But market speculation that the next rate rise would be 50 basis point was ill-founded and the bank was likely to stick to the more usual pattern of 25 basis point changes, he said.
Coleman saw rates heading up to 7.0 percent by the end of the year, whilst Lehman's Dicks saw rates around 7.5 percent, before peaking at around 8.25 or 8.5 percent next year.

Analysts said 90 percent of Brown's net fiscal tightening was aimed at companies, with the consumer sector escaping with only modest increases, such as higher rates of stamp duty on properties worth 250,000 stg or more and a cut in mortgage interest relief from April next year.

"These measures are unlikely to make much difference. If you wanted to use fiscal policy for demand management you would have to have hit the consumer a lot harder than this," said Ruth Lea head of the policy unit at the Institute of Directors.

But both Lea and Royal Bank of Scotland economist Marian Bell had some cold comfort for the new Chancellor. Both take the view that fiscal policy is a blunt tool for demand management and that interest rates are a much better way of cooling demand in any case.

Bell is also relatively sanguine on the interest rate front and does not see a rise next week. "We've seen a rate rise in each of the last two months and third in a row might look a bit strange," she said.
"The Bank will want to see some second quarter GDP numbers before it does anything further," she argued.
